Messages.Author: The Lasombra
Messages.Body:
Tomorrow we will elect the next President of the United States. The
result will have great consequences for the nation.

This election offers a choice is between two men with dramatically
different visions of the future. We have strong feelings about this
choice. But we feel even more strongly that all Americans, regardless
of political preference, have a stake in the outcome and should vote
in this critical election.

This is likely to be a close election. Your vote matters. Please use
it and make a difference.

Sincerely,

Jeffrey Thompson

Surely in a democracy it's time for us to quit being sentimental, and
say the question we settle in an election is not whether elites shall
rule, but which elite shall rule. - George Will

It is true that a vote for a libertarian, green, or independent
candidate will not result in that candidate being elected this time.
It is also true that such votes build a small amount of support for
third parties. Strictly speaking, it is not throwing the vote away,
it is spending it in the hope of developing a viable alternative to
the two party system. It is up to each individual voter to determine
whether voting for a given candidate is "worth it" given their
circumstances. See also: the electoral college and living in a non-
swing state (hello Massachusetts!).

There are also a lot of important questions down ballot. There are
state, national, and local reps running in contested races, and
referendum questions, and your vote regarding those things matters a
lot. Even in a state like mine, a vote for one of the two major
candidates matters, it just doesn't matter much.

Get to your polling place.

-dc

I was joking, but you are absolutely right. If I had voted in the
2000 election, it would have certainly been for a 3rd party candidate,
not because I thought they would win, but because my vote really
doesn't matter in Illinois as far as electoral votes go, and I wasn't
particularly interested in seeing either guy win.

This year, I really truly believe in one of the two candidates and
wanted to show my support even in such a small way as 1 vote. I don't
really hate the other guy (would have voted for him in 2000 or 2004
given the chance), but I really believe in my Senator.

I would really like to see a 4 party system consisting of fiscal
conservatives, evangelical conservatives, personal freedoms liberals
and socialist-leaning liberals, or something like that. And if voting
for the Green or Constitution or Libertarian Party (or whatever other
candidate) helps to loosen the hold of the 2 party system without
facilitating in the election of a candidate that you find really
distasteful, then more power to you!

I am a US citizen, and I agree almost 100% with Daneel's statement,
which I found neither ill-informed nor Anti-American, nor ignorant.

I understanding you are objecting to the characterization of the U.S.
President as a "figurehead", and to an extent, I agree with you. In a
relative sense, and compared to some other political leaders, the
powers of the U.S. President are quite substantial.

But it is not an issue of the specific powers of the U.S. President,
but an issue of the very nature of power. The United States
government is a vast vast institution, and the President is one man.
The President's vast powers are largely illusory, because if he bucks
the system, the system will chew him up and spit him out. Even if he
were a dictator, with absolute power, the principle would apply.

It's not that he cannot do good. He can do as much good as one good
man can do in a vast vast system that is far vaster than he is. I am
guessing, however, that the more actual good he does, the more he will
be perceived as a weak president. He can become a strong president
only by adapting himself to the needs of power, and that is where the
"power corrupts" principle enters the equation.

"All power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
Great men are almost always bad men." -- Lord Acton

If we are lucky, our new president will not be a great president -- he
will merely be a good one.

On Nov 7, 3:00 pm, Jeff Kuta <jeff.k...@gmail.com> wrote:
> The Commander in Chief of the entire United States military is a mere
> figurehead?

Did I say that? I thought I made clear that I did NOT consider him to
be a "mere figurehead".

> How do you think we got where we are today without serious action and
> serious consequences from those at the top?

I'm not sure what you mean by "serious action" or what you think the
issue is. Kings and Emperors come and go. They do what they do.
Most of what they do is wicked, and it does indeed have serious
consequences. And the World turns.

> If you want to claim that the President has little to do with changing
> economic conditions, I'm with you there.

I never claimed that. I expressed no opinion on that particular
point.

> People do tend to think the
> President has more influence there than he really does.

> But if you think the POTUS doesn't wield enormous individual power,
> real and symbolic, you're sorely mistaken.

Either that, or the "Enormous Individual Power" wields him. Man does
not become Superman, merely because he is made King. He remains a
man, with two arms, two legs, and one voice. If the POTUS doesn't
mind being corrupted by his power, which to a large extent means he is
controlled by his power, then yes, he can indeed wield "Enormous
Individual Power". But if he insists on being a good man, he may find
that the "Enormous Individual Power" slips through his fingers, or,
more likely, that he never manages to gain "Enormous Individual Power"
in the first place.

Of course, the US is, in theory at least, a democracy. A popular
leader could, in theory, continue to be an effective leader and a
decent person, to the extent that his power really comes from the will
of the common folk, who tend to be less wicked than elites. But such
a decent, popular, effective POTUS would not think of himself as
someone who wields "enormous individual power". He would think of
himself as the humble servant of those who put him in office.
